content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").

- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

## The consolidation tools

Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Put the open questions of the runs on the review queue.

Pick the tool by the job:

- To bring the record in line with a landing: the record-landing workflow (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`.
- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow. Its writer changes only a sentence that is false, stale or not the curator's. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
- To make entries read on their own, with their meaning kept: the clarity workflow. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is", and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
- To correct the entries that a review's findings name: the clarity workflow, with `findings.md` in each chunk's folder, in the form that its README gives. An entry changes only where a finding names it, and grows only by what the correction needs.
- To keep `fortress-repo`'s revival part short enough to read whole: the orientation workflow. Its update mode runs after each landing. Run its consolidate mode when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.

## INDEX and the gap ledger

- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.

# Plan: microGPT compiled on the JVM

The order Pavol approved on 2026-09-26 (P-33). The evidence under it is the inventory `coordinator/open-items-2026-09-26.md`.

## Where we stand

- **Runs.** microGPT runs under walk: its quick walk check gave both programs 7 of 7 at every landing from climb batch 11 to climb batch 32 and at both runs of climb batch 31 (each gate's `summary.txt`, its `# microgpt-walk` line; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-31/gate/summary.txt`; for run 2, its commit stage, `reviews/batch-31b-review.md`, section 4). The 52 team demos reach their end, except that `Generator2Demo` stops with `IntegerOverflow` on some of its random data, on the base too: 52 of 52 on the merged trees of climb batch 32 and of both runs of climb batch 31 at their gathers, and 51 of 52 on climb batch 30's (F-283; row 986; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-31/RECORD.md` and `compile-ladder/climb-batch-31b/RECORD.md`, "The tests on the merged tree"). Walk is not timed (`coordinator/PLAN-history.md`, "The timed pairs of the walk check dropped, 2026-10-23"). On the compiled path microGPT's 18 components stop at name resolution until the switch-over (F-97). In a scratch tree switched onto the one library, three small programs ran compiled, one that prints a line, one over an `Array1` and a dot product in the program's own loop; no matrix, none of the library's own array algebra and no microGPT (F-352). Nothing of it landed.
- **The live thread.** Phase 4, the switch-over: one library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks (P-37), the natives first (P-33). At the last landed gate, climb batch 31b's (`00dd16a891`, run 2 of climb batch 31, its gate on `4fdabc2ae8`), the distance is 0 and the checker count 0 over the fourteen components, with no crash row (F-53; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-31b/gate/`). Climb batch 29 built the numeral default and fold (P-173) and the strings (P-171) on both paths, and climb batch 29b rebuilt the numerals as the static numerals on both paths and in the specification (P-174, P-176). Climb batch 30 built the numerals' leftovers (F-348, F-349); on the compiled path, the join of every forked arm and the fork of a call's arguments, with a grain size of 16 in the one library's parallel range (P-175; F-350); and six repairs of the compiled transaction (F-351). Climb batch 32 built the model's notation: the signs `∑` and `∏` as accumulators and a postfix operator declared in an api (F-362); a superscript after a dotted access and after a parenthesised call (F-363); the checker's instantiation of a reduction that writes no static argument and of a generic function passed as a value (F-364, F-365); the numeral rule on both paths, so that `u = 0` is `true` for a zero `u` of `NN32` (F-366); under walk, a generic function as a value (F-367) and a typed array literal at the top level (F-368); and the compiled top-level tuple binding (F-369). Climb batch 31's run 1 built, on the compiled path, each inherited method written once and a body inherited through an api's trait (F-372), `label` and `exit` (F-373), `atomic` as an expression and an object's `var` field in a cell (F-374), the cast of `self` (F-377, F-225), and the Return Type Rule at an object type with the dispatcher's cast (F-75, F-376); and, under walk, its two repairs that come before the merge (F-375). Climb batch 31b, its run 2, built on the compiled path a method whose one parameter is a tuple (F-378) and a numeral that ends a block converted where it stands (F-380), and merged the five number types with their objects in the one library and walk (P-178; F-379); the prelude keeps its traits until its half is built by way (b) of fork H2, which P-178 settles (review-queue item 577, answered). What the two paths still do differently is in `reviews/batch-31-review.md`, section 1, "What the two paths still do differently after this run"; since run 2 they differ also in the five types' form (`reviews/batch-31b-review.md`, Part 5, 1). 373 of the library's 401 live bindings name helpers of `nativeHelpers/`, and `Reflect`'s 28 are the only ones that still name glue classes, since the numerals' 24 left with the old numeral types (F-299, F-32). Row 895 is closed, and the checker reads `System` whole on climb batch 28's rung S tree; but `System`, `File` and `Reader` are outside the fourteen, so no gate stage checks them (F-321, F-290; `reviews/batch-28-review.md`, section 6). The code generator refuses 17 declarations of the fourteen components in 5 kinds on run 2's landed code, measured on a patched scratch tree, since on the tree as it stands it stops three components whole at row 874; it refused 21 in 6 kinds before run 2, and the four of row 819 are emitted now (F-34; `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/planner/codegen-measure.sh`). Since climb batch 27's rung G it compiles a type assumption at a receiver, at a call whose every dispatched argument is one, and as a value, and since climb batch 28's rung T an object whose first supertrait is an imported api's trait (row 733) (F-320, F-325, F-338). P-160's two steps are built: walk's load check reads a program's generic operators between an array and a number beside a self-typed additive group's own (F-318), and `Number` has no `comprises` clause, `asFloat` or `=` (F-324). Of the readings under that zero, review-queue item 295 waits for his word, and items 309 and 326 are closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05 (learning) (row 844; F-308); climb batch 32's rung C closed row 731's checker gap (F-364; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-32/RECORD.md`, "Rows closed"). Their items for him are in `coordinator/review-queue.md` and in their lists below.
- **Probed, 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-13; nothing landed.** Eight probes and reviews ran outside any batch, each in scratch or by reading. The rehearsal of the switch-over met sixteen walls on the way to three small compiled programs against the one library (F-352; `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`). The plan review sorted them into walls that a test against the prelude can show today and walls that only the switch shows, and put two orders of the remaining work, the whole switch-over first or the model's slice first (`reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md`, sections 7.1 and 7.2). Probe Y showed one build serving both libraries, which the second order needs (F-353). The pure-Java microGPT is written and timed (F-355, F-356), and the first compiled loop against the one library is of the order of 100 times from Java (F-358). The carriers' review gives the ways in which a run-time class carries a built-in type (`reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`; F-359, F-379), and a probe merged the five number traits with their objects in scratch (F-361). Their rows are 988 to 1000 of the gap ledger. His decision of 2026-11-16 on the built-in number types is taken: each of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` is one `value object` under its own name, and walk's native number objects `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go, on both paths before the switch-over (P-178; review-queue items 371, 372 and 515, answered). The one library's half is built: climb batch 31b's rung O merged the five in the one library and walk (`f6e24650e7`; F-379), and the merge is phase 4's line on it. The prelude's half is in no run, and the prelude keeps its traits (row 1003); its way, fork H2, is settled by P-178: way (b), built once for both libraries (review-queue item 577, answered). His decision on the order of the remaining work is taken: the rest of the switch-over takes microGPT's slice first, one build serving both libraries by a second set of the run time's value classes (P-33; review-queue item 512, answered), and item 521, the form of that second set, now arises. One decision of his stands first and is not taken: the carriers of the built-in types that P-178 does not cover, `Boolean`, `Char`, `String` with `FlatString` and the Java-backed traits (review-queue item 513, with 514). The other questions of these sources are items 516 to 524, 526 and 527. Of the merge's, 516, 518 and 519 landed at the record's defaults with run 2 and stay open for his review (items 97 and 98 under "Pavol's answers"); 517 and 520 are in the queue's part (a), since run 1 closed their rows 997, 998 and 542.
- **Next.** Climb batch 31b, run 2 of climb batch 31, landed (phase 4's twelfth line) at `00dd16a891`, on his go of 06:39 UTC on 2026-11-17, which took its forks at the planner's defaults, and its post-batch review is committed (`257cae950`). Run 1's record-landing ended at 08:31 UTC that day. Run 2's record-landing routes the review's list, and then the orientation update and the skill update run (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing", steps 2 to 5); the batch after launches only after the skill step, unless he says otherwise (`reviews/batch-31b-review.md`, "The steps due before the batch after", 5). The code generator's count on the landed tree is taken: 17 (F-34; the same steps, 4). The coordinator's own steps before the batch after: the script's fixes of the review's process findings 1, 4 and 5 (the same steps, 6); and the two steps still owed from run 1, row 1049's expected-failure walk test and the trace of `compiler_tests/OverloadReturnObjectDomain.fss:26` (the same steps, 9). The review puts his words in this order: item 512, the order of the remaining work, which he answered at 12:34 UTC on 2026-11-17 with microGPT's slice first (P-33); then item 577, fork H2, the first item of the list for the batch after, which his decisions on file settle, as he said at 15:13 UTC that day: P-178's detail, the carriers' review's way D, gives way (b), built once for both libraries and sized by a probe; then item 572, which the coordinator took at 1a, the first rung of the batch after, for his review (the same steps, 7). Finding 1 of run 2's review, fork E2, holds nothing: it landed at its default (item 101 under "Pavol's answers"; review-queue item 586). Forks O3 and O4 landed at their defaults, for his review (items 97 and 98; review-queue items 518 and 519). The findings of climb batch 32's review stand at their defaults (items 86 and 88; review-queue items 525 and 529); its finding 2 he reviewed as landed on 2026-11-16 (review-queue items 528, 533 and 530, in the queue's part (a)), and the model's four diffs are applied at his word of that day (`5ba4f78ed3`; items 547 to 550, in (a)). The findings of climb batch 30's review stand at their defaults as landed (items 80 to 82). What comes after climb batch 31, the walls that only the switch shows, each met as one rung on `main` by P-33's order, waits on his decision on the carriers of the other built-in types (item 513), and item 521, the form of the second set of the run time's value classes, arises with it. The gap ledger's repair waits on review-queue items 265 and 267. What is in flight is `coordinator/BOOT.md`.

- Needed by: before the names batch (set by the landing workflow).

516. **Where do the five number objects live after the merge of the five number traits with their objects?** Question 1 of the merge probe. Either in `FortressLibrary`, with walk told by a table of five names which of that component's objects have native values, as the probe built it; or in `FortressBuiltin` beside `NN32` and `RR32`, with six private functions and the five types' api moved there.
   - Landed: `FortressLibrary`, with walk's table of the five names (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java:455-470`), by climb batch 31b's rung O (`f6e24650e7`), the record's fork O1. Default: as landed.
   - The other way: `FortressBuiltin`, which keeps walk's one rule, that a native component's objects are native.
   - Its cost: Staying: 126 lines net of library text and a table of five names in walk's Java. Moving: about 620 lines of objects and 50 of helpers, and the five types leave the api `FortressLibrary`.
   - Home: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/number-object-merge.md`, "What was built" and "Questions for the curator", 1; `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-31.md`, section 3, fork O1; `reviews/batch-31b-review.md`, section 2, O1; PLAN, phase 4, the merge's line
   - Needed by: no planned work (set by the landing workflow); the fork landed at its default with climb batch 31b, for his review.

518. **What does `round` of an `RR64` answer: a `ZZ64`, as it ran before the merge, or a `ZZ`, as P-68 gives (row 1000)?** Question 3 of the merge probe. Before the merge `trait RR64` declared `round(self): ZZ`, and its object `Float` declared `round(self): ZZ64` over a helper that answers a Java `long`; `Float`'s ran. Since climb batch 31b's rung O there is one declaration, `round(self):ZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:548`), over `simpleDoubleArith.doubleRound`, and the api still declares no `round` for `RR64`. `truncate` and the floor and ceiling brackets answer `ZZ64` (row 330).
   - Landed: `ZZ64`, one declaration, the body that ran before the merge, by climb batch 31b's rung O (`f6e24650e7`), the record's fork O3; P-68's rung after the switch-over still makes it `ZZ`, with `truncate` and the brackets. Default: as landed; the review recommended it (finding 3, 3a).

content.content:
The curator is the person in charge of the project. PLAN (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`) is the working plan: its phases, the curator's answers in the order the work needs them, and the parked items. `PLAN-history.md` holds, word for word, each line taken out of PLAN, under a heading for the landing that moved it. The review queue (`review-queue.md`) is the one home of each item that waits for the curator's word or review, numbered, in three parts: (b) consequential, (c) routine, (a) settled or stale. `INDEX.md` holds one line for each note. A landing is the commit that put a batch's merged work on `main`. An entry is one line of FACTS or POSITIONS under its permanent number.

## The problem

A batch has landed. PLAN still says where the work stood before it: its "Where we stand", the batch's own line in its phase, lines that the batch built or answered, and lines that no longer hold. The batch's items for the curator wait in PLAN's list for his review, or in no file. The review queue's head names the old next batch. Notes have no INDEX line. A sorter has listed what the record owes, one change per line, in `owed.md` in the run's folder. Each change has a number (C1, C2 ...), a home, a kind, a weight and its ground. Your homes are five: a PLAN line, PLAN-history, a review-queue item, an INDEX line, and a line of another note. The entries writer takes FACTS, POSITIONS, their histories and the gap ledger at the same time, in the same worktree.

## The question

For each change of `owed.md` whose writer is `routing`, what do PLAN, PLAN-history, the queue, INDEX or the note hold after it? Make the edit in the worktree, so that each file stands in line with the landing and nothing that it held is lost.

## Where the sources are

- `owed.md`, and the evidence beside it: `plan.md` (PLAN's headings with their lines, the lines that the batch added, and the other lines that name a changed entry or row), `cites.md` (the queue items and INDEX lines that name them), `rows.md`, `checks.md` (the notes without an INDEX line, and the citations of PLAN by line number) and `sources.md` (the queries of the post-batch review's routing part and of the batch record's items for the curator).
- The routing's rule: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#After the landing'`, its step 2.
- The form of a queue item: read the queue's head and three items of one of its themes (`facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md#When each item is needed'`, and a theme's section). The form of PLAN-history's landing sections: its last one, `## Climb batch N's landing, DATE`.
- The record itself. You read it only through `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`, `record.py` and `ledger.py`; in this session the first one runs, from the worktree: `'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, `'doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS'` for the items of a section that hold some words, `'index:WORDS'`, `'positions:WORDS'`, `'F-87'`, `'ledger:N'`. The Edit tool needs the lines that it edits read first: open only those lines, at the line numbers that the evidence or `facts-extract.sh` gives. You write no entry: entries are written only through `record.py`, from the entries writer's file.

## How each home changes

- **A line moved.** A line that the batch built or answered, or that no longer holds, goes to `PLAN-history.md` word for word: under the landing's heading, `## Climb batch N's landing, DATE` (DATE from `git log -1 --format=%cs LANDING`), and under the heading that it stood under in PLAN. Every line that leaves PLAN or changes in it stands there word for word, since `checks.sh` compares the two files line by line.
- **A line cut to a pointer.** An open line whose whole text another home holds (a queue item, a ledger row, an entry) becomes one line in PLAN: what is asked, its default, and a pointer to that home. Its old text moves as above.
- **The batch's own line** in its phase becomes one line, with its landing commit and its post-batch review. "Where we stand" states the landing. Both keep the form that `explorations/coordinator/tools/revival-page/update.py` parses, or the workflow's last stage stops: the batch's line opens ``- **Climb batch N**, phase P's ORDINAL batch, landed YYYY-MM-DD at `COMMIT` ``, with N as the record names the batch and a second run such as `31b` on a line of its own, and the live thread says ``At the last landed gate, climb batch N's (`COMMIT` ``.
- **A queue item.** Each item for the curator that no file holds becomes one, numbered after the queue's last number, in its theme's section, in (b) if it is consequential and in (c) if it is routine, by the kind that `owed.md` gives. It says what is asked, its default as the record states it or "no default on record", the other way, its cost, its home, and its "Needed by". A "Needed by" that the batch record or the review states is taken as stated. Any other is yours, and you mark it "(set by the landing workflow)". Each section's count and the head's counts follow the items.
- **A move to (a).** An item goes to "Answered by a decision of his" only with his word on that same item, cited with its time. A default that the coordinator or a batch took is not his word. That item stays open in (b) or (c), with the default as landed, since such a decision lands and then goes to him for review (the `coordinator` skill, "The curator's role and decisions", way 2). `queue-check.py` fails a new item in that section that names such a default, or his word on another item. An item goes to "Answered by a landed fix or a closed row" only with the commit or the row that made it moot.
- **An INDEX line** for each note that `checks.md` names without one: `` - `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
- **A citation of a moved line** by its line number, in PLAN, the queue, FACTS, POSITIONS or INDEX: repoint it. `checks.md` lists them.

You invent no default and no answer of the curator. Before you call an item open, search POSITIONS and INDEX for his answer. The boot note (`BOOT.md`) and the held list (`HELD.md`) are the coordinator's: you edit neither, and you name in your report each change that they need.

content.content:
**fork**
: Design question with more than one way forward.

**cross-area question**
: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.

**go**
: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work. A bare go, "go" with nothing named, starts the background work that you proposed, never a batch. A standing go covers a named series of work, and stands in this skill.

**ask**
: Message that puts one decision to the curator.

**hold**
: Decision that the work waits on until the curator answers.

**review list**
: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: one line for each item for the curator's later review, with a pointer to its item in the review queue once the queue holds it.

**interrupt**
: Stop of a turn by the stop button.

**process stop**
: End of the session's process, by the platform's cap, idleness or a VM restart. The platform restarts it in the same session.

**tokens written**
: Input tokens and tokens written to the prompt cache, as `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py` counts them.

**boot note**
: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.

**held list**
: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.

**model check**
: Stop hook `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, which raises an alarm after a turn of the coordinating session that ran on neither Opus nor Fable.

**git-check switch**
: Hook `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, which keeps the platform's git-check hook off.

## The standing goal

You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.

- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
- Keep your context for decisions. Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows, source and long reports to workers, and act on their summaries.
- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.
- Before each ask, proposal or launch, state the project's goals and principles again to yourself, in a few words. Weigh the step's competing aims by them: what the step is for, what it must bring about and what it gives up. Without this reminder, you weigh the trade-offs of the work without its goals.
- Take a worker's report as evidence, not as the list of work to do. Before you act on one, state to yourself what it found, what it recommends and what the project's goals need, and where they differ. Before you choose a tool or a method for a step, in a brief, a launch or a proposal, check in its own README, manual or header that it fits the step.

## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

The revival resolves the contradictions that the team left, by the evidence in the repository: the specification, the papers, the library and the code. The curator does not redesign the language, and decides a contradiction that the evidence leaves open, by the designers' intent. The curator's words show what the curator decided. They are not the ground of the design.

Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.

Weigh a team text by its provenance: who wrote it, in which role, such as a core designer or an outside contributor of the open-source years, and whether the team reviewed it or its author called it provisional. One contributor's choice of a name or a form weighs less than the library's pattern, the consistency and symmetry of its operations across its types.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it. An entry's history is part of that search, and is read before any claim about the entry's reasons, since the history keeps the ground and the curator's words that the entry's text leaves out.
- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.

The coordinator put no question to you first. The rule for a night when you are away decided each fork below: the fork took its default, and it is on your review list. The part "Run 2, rung by rung" has your words.

### What was held out

- **No rung was held out.** No default bends a decision of yours. No rung changes a line of the model program or of its helper files.
- **One piece of the merge waits: the prelude.** It is not designed. The section "The merge" gives the question that holds it.

## 3. The forks, with their defaults

**Consequential** means what the `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", gives: it reverses, bends or reads anew a decision on record; it touches microGPT's lines, speed or readability; it chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent; or it cannot be undone. On the night of the go the rule of `references/batch.md`, "The go", decides each fork: a fork takes its default and goes on the review list, and a rung is held out only where the default would reverse or bend a decision on record or change a model line.

### The consequential fork

None in a rung that runs. **Fork H2,** the way in which the compiler's prelude takes the form of P-178, was taken here as a choice among ways that the record does not settle; P-178's detail, way D, settles it: way (b). Neither way has a probe: the piece that needs it is in no run of this record (section 2, "The merge"; section 5, "The probes of 2026-11-16"). **Fork W** of the record as first drafted moved with rung N to climb batch 32 and landed there at (a).

### Forks the batch takes

Of the forks below only H2 (item 5) is consequential, and its default builds nothing. Each other fork builds within a decision on record or chooses where the record leaves an implementation open, and each can be undone.

1. **B1. One record, two runs.** Run 1 is M, K, L, A, V and X; run 2 is T, O and E on run 1's landed tree. **Default: so.** Way not taken: one run of nine rungs, in which M and T would edit `CodeGen.generateForwardingFor` and `dumpMethodChaining` together, O would be built without V's two repairs, and E could meet K at a returned value. The reason: `references/batch.md`, "The go".
2. **B2. A's two compiled tests join the atomic runs.** **Default: `AtomicExprCompiled` and `AtomicFieldCompiled`, three runs each at four threads.** The reason: each is a test of a race.
3. **B3. Of the rows that climb batch 32's review offered, and rows 1032 to 1035, four are built and the others wait.** Rows 1014 and 1030 are rung E; rows 1031 and 1013 are tried by a run, in E and in M; rows 1028, 1029, 1005, 1007, 1009, 1010, 1012, 1015 and 1035 wait for the batch after; row 1032 waits for review-queue item 552; rows 1033 and 1034 are no work of a batch. **Default: so.** Way not taken: a checker rung for rows 1028 and 1029 in run 1, about 0.7M, for two gaps that are no wall on the path to the switch-over.
4. **H1. Varargs is left out.** **Default: so; first rung once a program compiles against the one library.** Way not taken: a rung that compiles only a declaration whose body does not read the parameter, which no line of the library has. The reason: PROBES, section 2.
5. **H2. The prelude's half of the merge is in no run.** P-178 and P-37's exception ask that the prelude's number types take the form of a `value object` before the switch-over. The declaration alone compiles and then stops every compiled program, since the hand-written run-time class of each type extends a class that the code generator writes only for a trait (PROBES, section 8). **Default: it waits for a probe of the smaller way, in which the code generator writes for these objects what it writes for a trait today, and is then one rung; `NN32` and `RR32` of the prelude, which are traits there, go with it.** Way not taken: a rung tonight without a probe; or the larger way, a value object with a JVM payload in the code generator, which the switch-over needs and the carriers' review sized a
6. **S. The stable order of the code generator's output is not a rung of this batch.** **Default: so; M's choice is made by rule and shown under two hash modes; the order's own rung is in the batch after.** Way not taken: one more rung in run 1, which would edit the loop that M repairs and `OverloadSet`'s order. ## Decisions

1. **The value check passes every symbolic type** (fork V1). Ways not taken: make the symbolic type a value type where its bound is one, which changes what every later check of the type reads; override the check in `SymbolicType`, which needs the private method opened. Evidence: the probe's suite passed with the one line; `ant testSystem` passes.
2. **Where the shortcut would fire, the reading on declared domains decides, and anything but a named rule leaves the pair accepted.** Ways not taken: (a) withdraw the shortcut and let the check's ordinary flow run, in which a plain declaration better at a parameter without a symbolic type meets the team's Subtype Rule branch and row 785's refusal for an unwritten return type; (b) remove the shortcut for every pair, which is row 697 and refuses pairs of the library. Evidence: row 785; the brief's section, "the shortcut stays as it is for them".
3. **A more specific declaration that writes no return type is not judged at an object type.** Ways not taken: read its range as walk gives it, `Any`, which refused the brief's guard (seen in the first run after the edit); read it as `BottomType`, which changes `Simple_fcn` for every caller. No decision on record covers the unwritten return type; I acted on the brief's guard, and recorded the invalid pair that loads as row 1044.
4. **The new reading is added to the old one, not put in its place.** The old comparison, type parameters standing for themselves, is sound and settles results that mention no static parameter. Way not taken: the new reading alone; the old one is kept so that no pair read valid before is refused.
5. **The reading applies in `validOnDeclaredDomains` wherever the plain declaration lies inside the generic, not only where the shortcut would have fired.** So a plain declaration over a mix of object and trait types loads where it was refused. Way not taken: a flag that limits it to the shortcut's pairs, which would keep a refusal that the rule does not make.
6. **A `comprises` clause is not read** (fork V4). Row 550's pair at `ZZ64` stays refused.
7. **Two guards in two files, and a test of the value check's refusal added.** The brief names `XXXNonValueOfValue` as the test of the check; it is not (row 1045), so a plain test with a `load_exception_contains` key was written. The team's test is left as it is: it is beyond the files the section names.
8. **The Effect at changes.tex:2717 is not edited**: the section names the box alone.

- spec: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:531-674`, section "Declarations with Static Parameters" (the Meet Rule, and exclusion by existential reduction).
- precedent: `genericPairValid`, two own generics read on their declared domains, and `domainsExcludeTogether`'s existential reduction (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:894-918` and `:936` at the base; F-252, F-258).
- deviation: walk has no intersection type (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/EvalType.java:407-411` reads `A & B` as `A`), so the self parameter's intersection with the self-type parameter is read at the call site in `domainsExcludeTogether` (`OverloadedFunction.java:1081-1092`), as a second member checked with `excludesAtMeet`, not as a new case inside `excludesAtMeet`.
- deviation: a trait is read as self-typed only where its parameter's own bound is the trait at that parameter (`OverloadedFunction.java:845-867`); P-146's second form, a parameter bounded by another self-typed trait that the trait extends at it, is not read, so such a pair keeps the refusal.

## 10. Decisions

1. The pair is read by `genericPairValid` with the own generic first (`traitMethodPairValid`), not by a new reading of its own. Ways not taken: a separate reading for a function beside a trait method (more code, the same rules); `genericPairValid` in the order met (its `domainsExcludeTogether` takes the self members on `g` only). Ways not taken: a new case inside `excludesAtMeet` (walk has no intersection `FType` to dispatch on, `EvalType.java:407-411`); an intersection type in walk's model. Evidence: `EvalType.java:407-411`.

Way not taken: leave it, under which a function of the trait method's name and static parameters would get an empty fresh list and keep its refusal. Evidence: the two lists are equal for every earlier caller (`FGenericFunction.java:171-173`).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""plan-moves.py --root WT --base AT [--stale-at REV]: check that every line taken out of PLAN.md went to PLAN-history.md word for word, and list the PLAN lines that look stale.

A line taken out is a line of PLAN.md at AT, the commit that the worktree WT was made at, that the working
PLAN.md no longer holds, as a whole line: a line moved, cut to a pointer, or changed. Each must stand among
the lines that the working PLAN-history.md gained since AT, as many times as it went. PLAN-history.md only
gains: a line that it lost is a failure too. Blank lines are not counted. Prints the counts, the headings
that PLAN-history.md gained, and each failure; exit 1 on any.

Then, for information only (they never fail), the PLAN lines to look at, one `LOOK` line each with its
reason, read against the working review queue and the history of AT:
  settled   a list line whose own pointer, a sentence "Review-queue item 296.", names items that are each
            settled in the queue's part (a), and that names no item open in (b) or (c); it skips a line that
            already carries a cleanup's mark, "closed at the cleanup of DATE" in any of the queue cleanup's
            forms ("(closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05: learning)", "item 127, closed at the cleanup of
            2026-11-05: settled", "are closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05 (learning)"): the cleanup marked
            it in place, and moving it out of PLAN is PLAN's consolidation, not a landing's change
  list      a list line that names three or more items, some of them settled; or one that ties its items
            to a list of the queue's head (the queue's "Needed before the switch-over") and does not name
            the same items
  finding   a line `- Climb batch N's review, finding M ...` whose finding a commit in the history of AT
            names (`batch-N-review.md, finding M`, or "climb batch N's finding M"), where that commit
            changes a file outside the record: a half of the line may be built
With --stale-at REV, it reads PLAN.md and the review queue at REV, and the history of REV, prints only the
LOOK lines, and exits 0: evidence.py gives them to the sorter in plan.md.
"""
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""queue-check.py --root WT --base AT: the review queue's numbers, its "Needed by" lines and its counts.

The review queue, explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md, holds numbered items in three parts: (b)
consequential and (c) routine, the open items, as `N. ...`, and (a) settled or stale, as `- **N, ...`.
Each `### Theme (K)` heading counts its items. Checks the working file against the one at AT, the commit
that the worktree WT was made at:
  numbers   each item number at AT is still in the file; the new numbers follow the last one at AT, one by one
  needed    each open item that is new, or that moved into (b) or (c), has a "Needed by:" line
  sections  each theme heading's count equals the items under it
  head      the head's "**Counts**, N open items ..." line equals the open, consequential and routine items, and the lines
            under it, one per kind of need, add up to it
  answered  each item new in (a)'s "Answered by a decision of his", filed there or moved there since AT, cites his
            word on that same item: a POSITIONS entry, a time or an answer of his, and before its "Home:" no default
            taken without him ("at its default", "by the coordinator", "the coordinator's call") and no word of his
            on another item ("on item 310"). A default that the coordinator or a batch took leaves the item open in
            (b) or (c), landed and then reviewed (the coordinator skill, "The curator's role and decisions", way 2).
Prints each failure and one line per check; exit 1 on any failure.
"""
